header.incumbent: Homegrown billing system, built by a guy who left
header.tag_why: The CFO froze all new vendor projects after a missed Q3. The deal was exposed to that freeze because, for about a month, Owen had been asking for a payback number of their own to take to Diane, and he never got it.

evidence.excerpt: Their VP of Product, Owen, had wanted to rebuild billing for a while.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: The billing system is homegrown, built by a guy who left, and every pricing change takes them a quarter.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: He wanted it done before they launched a new pricing tier, but the tier didn't have a date either.
evidence.label: fact

trigger.insight: No event forced this evaluation. It started as one executive's long-standing wish, and its only deadline was tied to a pricing tier that had no date. A deal without a forcing event needs a quantified cost of waiting to survive, and the rep never built one. The engineering lead's renewal-season rule was a real date that could have set the timeline, but nobody used it that way.
trigger.messaging: When a deal is inbound and has no deadline, open with what each quarter on the homegrown system costs, not with capability, so the urgency exists before finance looks at it.

evidence.excerpt: The CFO, I guess? Diane.
evidence.label: opinion

evidence.excerpt: Owen told me. I never spoke to her.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: No. Owen said he'd bring her in at the end.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: We only ever talked to product and engineering.
evidence.label: fact

decider.insight: The person who held the budget was never in a meeting. Everything we know about her rests on Owen's word. Letting the champion keep the CFO for 'the end' meant finance only ever met us through a generic deck. Whether Diane ever saw a business case for this project is not established.
decider.messaging: Build a CFO-facing billing asset (cost of the homegrown system, payback period, migration risk) that a champion can forward. Ask to put it in front of finance before sending paper.

evidence.excerpt: There wasn't one. It was us against doing nothing.
evidence.label: opinion

evidence.excerpt: Owen never looked at anybody else, as far as I know.
evidence.label: opinion

evidence.excerpt: Toward the end Owen started asking for things for finance.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: 'do you have something that shows payback?'
evidence.label: quote

competitor.insight: The competitor was the status quo, and the status quo wins by default unless someone puts a price on it. The shift in Owen's questions toward finance was the buying signal that the deal had moved to a money decision. It was answered with generic material. That there was no other vendor is only 'as far as I know'.
competitor.messaging: Against status quo, position on the cost of doing nothing in the customer's own figures, because that is what replaces a competitor comparison.

evidence.excerpt: Reaction: the billing demo. Changing a price in a few clicks, trials, proration.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: 'that's a quarter of roadmap in five minutes.'
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: 'we're not trying to grow revenue with billing, we're trying to stop it being a tax on the roadmap.'
evidence.label: quote

message.insight: The demo landed with product and engineering because it turned their pain, roadmap time, into minutes. Our revenue-growth framing (M7) did not just get silence; Owen rejected it outright, and the rep first claimed nothing fell flat. The audience we won over was never the audience that could fund the project.
message.messaging: For replacing homegrown billing, swap M7's 'grow revenue' for roadmap and engineering time given back, and translate 'a quarter of roadmap in five minutes' into a cost figure finance can read.

evidence.excerpt: They missed their number in Q3 and she put a hold on all new vendor projects.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: 'I can't get this past Diane without a number that's ours.'
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: We were going to set up a session to build one. Then Q3 closed.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Before that we were in procurement. Well, we'd sent paper.
evidence.label: fact

decided.insight: The freeze ended the deal, but the deal was exposed to it because the business-case session still had not happened about a month after Owen asked for payback. The rep's 'we were in procurement' shrank to 'we'd sent paper' under questioning. Paper went out before the one thing Owen said he needed to get past Diane existed.
decided.messaging: Make a customer-specific payback number the gate before paper on billing deals, and offer the build session the same week the champion asks.

evidence.excerpt: The number. Their own. What the homegrown system costs them.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: some landlord subscriptions lapse because the card fails and nobody chases it.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: We never added it up.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: We had a doc for that. He wanted to talk to someone who'd done it.
evidence.label: fact

gaps.insight: The missing proof was not a product gap. It was an unbuilt calculation and, possibly, a reference. Lapsed subscriptions from failed cards that nobody chases is lost money, the kind of 'on fire' cost that answers Diane's rule. It also maps directly to M10, and it was mentioned once and never pursued. On migration, a doc was not enough; Owen wanted a peer, and the transcript does not say whether one was ever offered.
gaps.messaging: Pair M6 with a fill-in cost-of-homegrown-billing calculator (engineering time, billing errors, revenue lost to unchased failed cards via M10). Back migration claims with a reference customer who moved subscriptions without re-collecting cards.

evidence.excerpt: 'we're not trying to grow revenue with billing, we're trying to stop it being a tax on the roadmap.'
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: 'if it isn't on fire, it isn't funded.'
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: nice to have.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: 'we don't touch billing before renewal season.'
evidence.label: quote

language.insight: Product spoke in opportunity cost ('tax on the roadmap'), and finance, at two removes, spoke in urgency ('on fire', 'nice to have'). Our pitch spoke in revenue growth, which neither side used. Nobody turned the roadmap tax into fire. The rep says, as their own read, that probably nobody told Diane what it was costing.
language.messaging: Use 'billing shouldn't be a tax on your roadmap' with product. Give finance a dollar figure that makes the homegrown system 'on fire' rather than a 'nice to have'.

gaps.question: What was the deal size (ACV)?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Renee what ACV was on the paper that was sent.

gaps.question: Who made the final call, and how do you know?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Owen whether Diane ever saw anything about this project before the freeze, and whether the freeze email came from her.

gaps.question: Did Owen consider any other vendor or an internal rebuild?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Owen directly whether anyone else, including an in-house rewrite, was on the table.

gaps.question: Was a reference customer for the migration ever offered or arranged?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Renee whether Owen was connected to a customer who had migrated subscriptions without re-collecting cards, and if not, why not.

gaps.question: Which part of our pitch got silence?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Renee what finance-oriented material reached Owen besides the general ROI deck, and how he reacted to it.

gaps.question: Why will this come back next year, and when does the freeze lift?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Renee for evidence behind 'it'll come back next year', and ask Owen when vendor projects reopen and whether that falls before or after renewal season.

close.rep_takeaway: When the champion starts asking for things for finance, the deal has become a money decision. Build their own number within days, not a month, using what they have told you (engineering time, billing errors, lapsed subscriptions), and get it in front of the CFO before paper goes out. 'It's timing' is only the full story if the business case already existed when the freeze hit.
